desc: Los Alamos is the first place the United States convened scientists to discuss unexplained objects over its own nuclear installations, and it is the laboratory that confirms it. On 16 February 1949 a conference was held at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory on the green fireballs then appearing over the New Mexico weapons complex; attendees included Laboratory Director Norris Bradbury, Edward Teller and Frederick Reines, together with representatives of the FBI, the Atomic Energy Commission and the US military. LANL's own National Security Research Center published this in November 2024, stating that it holds the conference minutes, that its senior archivist receives several UFO-related FOIA requests every year, and that the Center does not appear to hold materials on Project Twinkle although not all of its millions of items are searchable. In December 1949 Project Twinkle was established as a network of observation and photographic stations and never fully implemented. Newly declassified records on the 1949 conference were publicised in July 2026 in the wake of the PURSUE releases. In April 2026, filmmaker Jeremy Corbell announced a trove of documents said to have been provided by the son of a deceased former LANL cybersecurity chief, forming the basis of the documentary 'Sleeping Dog' and alleged to include material on a secret 1991 UFO meeting at the laboratory. LANL is administered by Triad National Security, LLC and was funded at approximately 3,918.3 million dollars in FY2024 - the second-largest FFRDC in the country. It is a contractor-operated laboratory whose archives are not agency records, which is why a laboratory blog post is currently a better source on the 1949 conference than any FOIA response.

dossier.narrative:
The board carries this laboratory for the ordinary reasons first. It hosted a conference on 16 February 1949 on the green fireballs, attended by Laboratory Director Norris Bradbury and Frederick Reines among others, which is documented by the laboratory itself rather than by the literature about it. Its senior archivist has said on the record that the institution receives several FOIA requests a year on unidentified aerial phenomena, which is a rare thing for an institution to say about itself and is the reason a `custody` reading of this node is defensible at all.

What brought it onto the top-level map is narrower and sharper. The Lazar account stands or falls on whether he was what he said he was, and the only contemporaneous documentary thread in his favour runs through here. On 27 June 1982 the Los Alamos Monitor put him on its front page. A 1982 internal telephone directory lists his name. Taken together they are routinely presented as proof of employment at the laboratory.

They are not that, and this node exists partly to say so precisely. The directory's own terms state that it covers outside contractors as well as staff, and a 1996 taped interview with a former colleague places him under Kirk-Mayer, a contractor, which is why `kirk-mayer` is now a node in its own right with an edge to this one. The board's rule, written as a claim on this node rather than left to a reader to work out, is that his connection is to be stated as named in a directory and never as employed by. That is a smaller claim than either his supporters or his critics usually make, and it is the one the documents support.

The laboratory has made no statement about him in anything opened here, and none is asserted. The edge from this node to `bob-lazar` is Tier 3 for exactly that reason.

dossier.whatItIs: Los Alamos National Laboratory, the Department of Energy federally funded research and development centre at Los Alamos, New Mexico, administered by Triad National Security, LLC since 9 June 2018 and receiving approximately $3,918.3 million in FY2024. It is the laboratory that built the first nuclear weapons, and on this board it appears in three unrelated capacities: as the host of a documented 1949 conference on the green fireballs, as an institution whose own archivist says it fields several UFO-related FOIA requests a year, and as the workplace named in the single most contested credential claim in the subject.
dossier.whyImplicated: It joined this map with the Lazar cluster of 18 September 2026, and it is the node where that cluster's central factual question actually lives. Bob Lazar's account requires a documented scientific career, and the one contemporaneous document that appears to supply it is a Los Alamos artefact: the 27 June 1982 front page of the Los Alamos Monitor, which reports on him as a laboratory-connected physicist, and a 1982 internal telephone directory that lists his name. Both are real, both were opened, and both are narrower than the use made of them. The laboratory is therefore not a bystander here. It is the place where the strongest evidence for the claimant and the strongest qualification of that evidence sit on the same pair of pages.
